questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I sought a combination of interesting academic opportunities and a location that excited me. Victoria in Canada definitely worked for me in that regard.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: More details below. In short - it was fantastic.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The social elements of the introduction were really good, with lots of opportunities to connect and make friends. There were these intro days where there were presentations, icebreaker events, and so on. When it came to actually going to school, that was a bit trickier. We didn't get an introduction to the platforms we were going to use to find information on classes and how attending classes actually worked. Weirdly the international student center weren't really able to help with school technical stuff, like changing classes, but could instead only help with visa stuff and social arrangements.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I just got the emails and then we figured stuff out as it came.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: You need to get started early. Around June/July, I went on the UVIC Off-Campus Housing on Facebook and started writing to every place that made sense. I got a decently priced room close to UVIC (820 CAD / Month) in a house with 4 other roommates. Making a post about yourself with a picture + budget also worked for my friends. Those who started looking late got places that were either expensive or far from Campus, and being close to campus is a massive +.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Being able to walk to campus is awesome. Buses do work ok and biking is also very doable - but since a lot of stuff and social things take place on campus, it's just nice being close. 

Try to find a place with other UVIC students if you can. While they might be a bit younger than you (since they often start uni at 18), it was in my experience more fun than having to live with 'adults' where there were noise limits and less possibility of hosting a party or having friends over.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
UVIC will send you some emails that guide you on how to register. 

It's important to send the registration application for every course - even the ones that you think you should be able to get based on what you are studying. If it's not a first year course, i'd send an application to take that course just to be sure.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I made a mistake in one of my registrations and over the summer it took really long for them to get back to me about the issue.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up getting all the courses i wanted, but it was a lot of work.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
In the full list of courses, some are only available in fall and some only in spring. Also take 5 courses even though you just need 4, and drop the course you like the least. 

I took one online course - ecology and conservation of whales, and while online courses rarely work, this one was actually really good.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Course levels are similar or maybe a little lower than Uni of CPH, but structurally very different. You have a lot more homework and stuff to turn in, all of it being graded. You can end up having grades from all the stuff you turned in is good enough for you to be able to skip the final exams.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Generally, you are guided much more through the course material, being quizzed and tested, so they know that you are doing readings and homework. 

UVIC has a super cool Indigenous programme that I recommend. Just be aware that you are not taught in a conventional western way - and while it can be difficult to wrap your head around, I found it super valuable.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Biodiversity of BC 
Geography of BC 
Indigenous Studies 101
Ecology and Conservation of Whales

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I recommend all my courses. 

Biodiversity of BC - great professor with some really fun projects throughout the course. One being that you have to collect iNaturalist observations. Was an easy course to get through and attending lectures was not mandatory.  
Geography of BC - This course with -Name Redacted- was the closest to a Danish uni course of the courses I had. There was a lot of reading and high expectations for you to understand the course material. Great course if you want to understand BC as a place. 
Indigenous Studies 101 - Fantastic course that challenged you to consider your privileges, perspectives, history and your role as someone contributing to science. The course is taught by -Name Redacted-, who is an Indigenous woman and matriarch.  
Ecology and Conservation of Whales - Fun, easy and interesting course that happened online.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are generally as expensive or more compared to Denmark. 

Traveling on Vancouver Island in the summer - super expensive, book stuff as far in advance as you can. 
Traveling in the off-season is significantly cheaper, and you don't have to book stuff way ahead of time. Do it a week or two before, ideally.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many clubs to join and things to do - so many that you won't be able to do everything that you want to. I joined the running, outdoor, and climbing clubs.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is pretty much everything. Taylor Swift club, Clubs for people from different countries, diving, caving, reading, knitting, dog petting, idk you name it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Bad weather: 
Go to downtown for: board game cafe (amazing place), axe throwing, Lucky Mondays (the night to go out in Victoria - no joke at Lucky Bar), Darcys for live music, haunted mini golf. Browse outdoor stores (MEC is the best). Boulderhouse is fun for climbing and much better than CARSA (campus climbing). You can go to the movies on Campus or downtown. Munro's books is great too. Browse Market Square. 

Good weather: Go to Mt. Douglas (panorama view of the city), go swimming (it's cold but safe and amazing all year), or go to East Sooke Regional Park or Goldstream (has salmon run and Indigenous traditional fishing). Run around Elk/Beaver Lake. Go on a whale watching trip (expensive but worth it 100%). Join social/sports events on campus - like frisbee on the lawn. Go surfing at Sombrio.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Here's my priority list
1. Tofino - go surfing and camp there. Book everything (camping spot, surfboards, tours) well in advance. Ideally, 6 months before or as soon as you have a group of friends to join you. There are also group trips arranged by UVIC that go here. 
2. Port Renfrew - you can go on a day trip or sleep there a couple of nights. This is where i saw a black bear and it was amazing. 
3. Mt. Washington and Strathcona - Bring your best hiking gear and go on the most amazing mountainous hikes. Lots of trails starting at Strathcona Park Wilderness Centre. If you sleep out here, be experienced or bring someone who is. There are bears and mountain lions here and weather that can turn dangerous. Bring bearspray. 
4. Cape Scott - super far away from Victoria, but so wild and untouched. You can surf and hike here. 
5. East Sooke - close to Victoria. 

It's generally hard to go somewhere on that island that isn't pretty amazing. Get a car and go!!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As everyone speaks English here and are generally very friendly and helpful, I don't think you're ever going to find yourself in a bad situation here. Some things work differently, like buying alcohol or having a campfire. You'll figure it out - nothing to be stressed about.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs and be open, but don't force yourself or push yourself too far. Almost every single one of my friends were exchange students or not locals and I had a fantastic time socially. Every time I felt like doing something, there was always someone who wanted to join, or there was an invite open for something. Being back home, things are much slower.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Canadians can sometimes over-promise in order to be polite and friendly. They might say we'll do this or that, but when it really comes to it, they might just have said it to be polite. So don't stress about it if it falls through

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Canadians were unrelenting in their friendliness. We had someone fix a road for us on the way to Cape Scott, people sharing stories at bars, people offering to help in all kinds of ways, and actually following through. We met an older couple on a mountain, and she let us see the mountain cabin she was staying in and left beer for us + invited us to visit her home. The most extreme cases of Canadians being friendly happened when we were on trips to remote little towns, where people were eager to give tips, share stories, and help out. Be ready for friendly small talk everywhere and just embrace it and learn new things and meet people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get a car or some way to transport yourself and your friends. I bought a car after two weeks and sold it a week before I went home. It's a pretty simple process. You need a driver's license (Danish is ok - I brought an international license too, but never used it) and either CAD cash or a way to transfer money relatively quickly (I got a Canadian bank account ahead of time to make it easier). Then you find a car on FB marketplace or wherever,  check the car, and go to an ICBC (state car insurance office), and they handle the transfer from the previous owner to you. You have to pay tax based on the price you pay for the car, but you can agree on a lower official sale price with the seller. I paid 5000 CAD for my car, about 1100 for taxes and insurance for 6 months, and I sold the car for 4000 CAD. 

You can also use Turo (private rental program) or register with EVO (do it through UVIC booths if you can and get a discount) 

Having a car opens up the island and lets you explore more easily.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I focused on enjoying my courses, focusing on topics I enjoyed and spending less time on stuff I didn't find interesting. I got good grades with this strategy and avoided feeling stressed out and kept my energy for going on super fun group trips.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Having amazing outdoor experiences with great new friends while studying unique courses in a new way.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I had 1 week where I had several projects due at the same time and was a little stressed due to that. The biggest challenge was perhaps the FOMO from all the amazing opportunities that there were too many of. Reflecting on the trip, I'm very satisfied with the things I did. So know you can't do everything and that's ok.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: All the work with signing up for courses, application processes, expensive plane tickets, and tricky housing stuff - getting through that will reward you with months of amazing experiences. I can't recommend going to Victoria enough.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
